title: Passed together: one vote list for many files
question: How many money files, and how many dollars, pass on a vote list identical to that of other files decided the same day?
finding: 2,983 of the 3,483 final votes (85.6%) sit in groups of 5 or more money files decided on the same day with the identical line-up of votes, naming $54.60 billion of the $66.59 billion in all titles. There are 312 such groups, on 303 of the 429 meeting days with a final vote on a money file; the largest is 44 files on 8 December 2015 (11 to 0, $886.2 million named). Only 134 files (3.8%) have a vote list no other money file shared that day, and 69 of those had a no. None of the 117 groups of ten or more contains a no vote. The one direct check on disk points to separate votes. In the minutes of the 14 Board meetings read for votes missing from the vote pages (133 of the 136 Board roll calls taken from them are dated 13 April 2016 to 26 July 2016), money files appear 133 times: 95 under “new business”; 25 under “unfinished business”; 13 under “committee reports”; none under the consent agenda, and every vote read is printed under its own item. 88 of the final votes in these groups were read from those minutes.
how: Final votes on money files are grouped by date and by the exact list of how each member is printed (aye, no, excused, absent). A group is every money file with the same date and the same list; files of other kinds decided that day are not counted, so the true lists are longer. The table shows the largest groups. The vote pages do not mark which items were on a consent agenda: only 2 action texts in the whole table mention the word.
limits: A consent agenda would look like this in the record, and so does a run of separate unanimous votes; both are ordinary. The Rules of Order provide for the first: “The Consent Agenda will be acted upon by a single roll-call vote of the Board.” The rule covers routine matters needing no further discussion, and any member can have an item taken off that agenda and heard separately. The record cannot tell one roll call covering many files from separate votes that came out the same: when every member is present and votes aye, any two votes that day look identical. So the figure is an upper bound on what passed in one motion, not a count of it, and where the minutes have been read the files were voted item by item under the ordinary agenda headings; that check covers a few months of 2016 and may not hold for other years. 2,942 of the 2,983 files in these groups have a recorded committee recommendation before the Board vote. Of the 770 files of $10 million or more introduced since 2019, 650 carry a report by the Board’s Budget and Legislative Analyst among their attachments, so a vote with no dissent can follow written scrutiny at the committee stage. Dollar figures are the totals named in file titles: an agreement amended twice is counted at each new total, rent and accepted grants are money coming to the City as well as money going out, and budget ordinances name no single figure, so a sum of title dollars measures what the titles name, not money spent. For 332 roll calls the Clerk’s vote page says “by the following vote” and lists no member, 306 of them dated 2016-04-13 to 2016-07-26; 315 were read instead from the vote lines in the Clerk’s published minutes of the same meeting, and 17 remain without member votes and are counted nowhere here. 1 money file (160358) whose final passage is among them is left out of the counts, and none is counted as unanimous. 104 of the final votes counted here were read from the minutes. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
